transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist here. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Well, they sent me here from occupational health at my job. They're saying my weight is dangerously low for someone running presses and doing fabrication all day. But honestly... I just thought I was getting leaner and more disciplined.
Have you been deliberately eating less food or restricting what you eat in order to lose weight?

Well, yes. Most days I... I just keep it to coffee before the early shift. Then maybe half a protein bar on my lunch break, and a small bowl of vegetables after yoga. I just find that eating any more than that makes the whole day feel completely out of control.
When you look at yourself in the mirror or think about your body, do you feel like you look overweight or larger than you actually are?

Yeah, I do. I mean... if I catch my reflection in a shop window, or even just looking in the bathroom mirror, all I can focus on is my stomach and my thighs. They just look too big to me. And honestly, once I see that, it kind of... it can ruin how I feel about myself for the entire rest of the day.
Besides restricting your food intake, do you do anything else to try to control your weight or prevent weight gain—such as making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or exercising excessively?

No, I don't do any of that. I don't make myself throw up or take laxatives, and I wouldn't say I exercise excessively. I mean, I do yoga most evenings, but that's just to stretch out my back after being on the shop floor all day. It's not really about burning calories. So, no, it's really just the food thing.
How long have you been eating this little—just coffee, a protein bar, and vegetables each day? And during that time, how much weight have you lost?

I'm not entirely sure, to be honest. It... it kind of just became my normal routine over time, so I don't have an exact timeline for when it got exactly this strict. 

And as for the weight... I don't actually weigh myself, so I don't have a number for you. I mean, I know I've lost weight because I can tell by how my work clothes fit now, but I really couldn't tell you how many pounds it's been.

Do you know roughly what you weigh now, or what your BMI is? And has anyone—like your doctor or occupational health—told you specifically what your current weight is or whether it's considered dangerously low?

Well, I don't know my exact weight or my BMI. But... occupational health actually sent me here because of that. They said my weight is dangerously low for the kind of work I do—running presses and doing fabrication all day. I was pretty surprised by that, honestly. I just thought I was getting leaner and, you know, more disciplined. I didn't think it was dangerously low.

Can you tell me your height? And do you happen to know what you weighed before you started restricting your eating, compared to what occupational health or anyone else has told you that you weigh now?

I'm about 5 foot 4. 

As for the weight... I really don't know what I weighed before I started eating less. I haven't owned a scale in years, so I just don't have a baseline number to give you. 

And with occupational health, they didn't actually tell me the exact number when they weighed me. Or if they did, I didn't catch it. They just looked at the scale, told me it was too low for me to be operating the presses safely, and told me I needed to come here. So I honestly don't have any of those numbers for you.

When occupational health weighed you, do you remember approximately what the number on the scale said, even if you didn't catch it exactly? Or can you describe how you looked or felt—for instance, do people comment on how thin you are, or have you noticed things like feeling cold easily, your period stopping if applicable, or feeling dizzy or weak?

Like I said, I really didn't see the number on the scale at all. I wasn't looking at it. 

As for the rest of it... no, I haven't really noticed any of those things. People at the shop don't comment on my weight. We wear heavy protective gear for fabrication anyway, so you can't really see much of my shape. I don't feel dizzy or weak. I mean, running the presses is hard physical work, so I get tired by the end of the shift, but that's just normal for the job. 

I haven't noticed being unusually cold, and... well, I haven't really paid much attention to my cycle, to be honest. I just haven't had any of those problems you're describing.

I understand you didn't see the scale reading at occupational health. But based on how your clothes fit now compared to before, and thinking about your body overall, would you say you're noticeably thin—thin enough that someone might be able to see your bones or ribs fairly easily if you weren't wearing your work gear?

I don't really know. I mean, my clothes still fit fine. I wear the same jeans and shirts I've had for a while. I haven't noticed them being super loose or anything. 

As for seeing my ribs or bones... I don't think so. I don't spend a lot of time looking in the mirror, honestly. I just shower, get dressed, and go to work. I haven't noticed looking noticeably thin or bony. I just look like me.

I know occupational health didn't tell you the exact number, but do you think you could call them or check any paperwork they gave you to find out what weight they recorded when they weighed you? That number would really help me understand what's going on.

I didn't get any paperwork from them to take with me. They just sent a note over to HR saying I wasn't cleared for the floor and needed an evaluation. I suppose I could try calling the clinic, but I don't know if they'd just give me that information over the phone. I can ask them, though, if you really need it.
If you're 5 foot 4, do you have any sense of what you might weigh now—even a rough estimate, like whether you're somewhere around 100 pounds, 110 pounds, 120 pounds, or something else?

I really couldn't give you a number. Like I said, they sent me here from occupational health because they said my weight is dangerously low for someone running the presses and doing fabrication all day. But I don't know what the scale said. I honestly just thought I was getting leaner and more disciplined.
When you look at your arms or legs, can you easily see the outline of your bones—like your shoulder blades, elbows, or hip bones—when you're not wearing heavy work gear?

I mean, I guess I can see my collarbones and maybe my elbows a bit more than I used to, but... I don't really think it's anything extreme. I'm just on my feet all day, moving metal around, so I figured I was just getting more toned. I haven't really noticed my hip bones or anything sticking out like you're saying. I just look normal to me.

I know you haven't seen the exact number, but occupational health clearly flagged your weight as dangerously low for your job. At 5 foot 4, would you say you weigh somewhere around 100 pounds or less, or do you think you're probably closer to 110 or 115 pounds?

Like I mentioned a minute ago, I really can't give you a good guess on whether it's 100 or 110. I just don't know. The only reason I'm here is because occupational health made a big deal about it, saying it was dangerously low for someone running the presses and doing fabrication work all day. But I still just don't see it that way. I've been working hard to be more disciplined, and I honestly just thought I was getting leaner.

You mentioned your clothes still fit the same and you don't look noticeably thin to yourself. But occupational health was concerned enough about your weight to refer you here and say it's dangerously low for your job. Do you think it's possible that you're actually lighter than you realize—perhaps in a range where occupational health would be genuinely worried about you operating heavy machinery safely, even if you don't see it that way yourself?

I hear what you're saying, but... I just don't think so. My family keeps saying I look sick, and yeah, the shop nurse acted like it was some kind of emergency when she sent me here. But I keep telling them all the same thing: I’m still working double shifts on the floor, I'm still running, and I'm getting things done just fine. If my weight was really that low or dangerous, I wouldn't be able to do all of that. So it just can’t be that serious.
